catalog_quote: [p.33, sec. 4.2 PWB phonological word] Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic—a word may consist of one or one and a half syllables. In the latter case a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable, a structurally impoverished unit that is constructed from a restricted set of segments. The minorsyllable typically consists of an oral stop or fricative of unmarked phonation type, an epenthetic ([a] or schwa-like) vowel, and may be closed by a nasal or rhotic. [p.28, Oi profile sec. 3.7] The minorsyllables are robust, with Oi frequently preserving Cər and Cən types. The minorsyllable vowel, whether phonemic or epenthetic, tends to be clearly vocalised as [a]. [Daniell 2020:4, Inthii Oy] Syllabic nasals are considered minor syllables because they resemble other minor syllables in duration and intonatory patterns, i.e. the main syllable being of a relatively higher pitch than the minor syllable.

(only scanned spacing differs). The following p.34 continues 'Sesquisyllabism is typical…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Oy words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (minor syllable + main syllable); the word-final main syllable is the stressed one, the preceding minor syllable is reduced (restricted onset set, epenthetic [a]-like vowel, lower pitch and no vowel-quality contrasts). Stress is thus fixed on the final (main) syllable and not contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Sidwell & Jacq note a small number of WB words with a phonemic (non-epenthetic) minor-syllable vowel before r, l, j, w, h (type Cə.RV(F)), still with the main syllable final; Daniell 2020 notes Lao loans and compounds but says nothing about their prominence.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word in citation form (elicited word lists). The Sidwell & Jacq sentence is phrased for West Bahnaric languages generally ('Most WB languages'), in a handbook whose Oi profile (pp.26-28, authors' own 1998/2002 field data) analyses Oi in the same mainsyllable/minorsyllable terms; Daniell 2020 supplies Oy-specific acoustic support (main syllable higher F0) but never uses the word 'stress'.
new_statements.identity_note: Sidwell & Jacq 2003 call the language 'Oi' (profile sec. 3.7, data from Ban Lagnao to Ban The, Ban Sok, Ban Inthi); their stress sentence (p.33) is phrased for West Bahnaric languages as a group, not Oi alone. Daniell 2020 describes the Inthii (Ban Inthi, Sanamxay District) variety of Oy specifically. Both = Glottolog oyyy1238 / ISO oyb (which since 2017 also subsumes former Jeng [jeg] and Sok [skk]).

sources.note: Oi profile sec. 3.7 pp.26-28: mainsyllable/minorsyllable inventories, robust minorsyllables with [a]-like vowel; no Oi-specific stress sentence. Sec. 4.2 p.33 (PWB phonological word): 'Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic.. a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable, a structurally impoverished unit' -- i.e. word-final main syllable carries stress (family-level statement, authors' own WB/Oi fieldwork).

sources.note: The word 'stress' never occurs. p.4 sec.3.1: minor syllables are identified by 'duration and intonatory patterns, i.e. the main syllable being of a relatively higher pitch than the minor syllable' with F0 measurements (209 vs 235 Hz, 210 vs 229 Hz); words are monosyllables or minor+main sesquisyllables with epenthetic minor-syllable vowels. Defers to Daniell 2019 thesis for the full synchronic phonology.
